newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tietmeyer - stability, not prestige, key to EMU.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer - stability, not prestige, key to EMU.

text.p: Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer, stressing the importance of genuine convergence for European monetary union, said on Friday that countries must not be allowed to enter EMU on a political ticket.
Speaking in the northern German city of Muenster, Tietmeyer said, "Only maturity in terms of stability policies, and not political prestige, can govern the selection of countries."
The Bundesbank has in the past expressed some nervousness about the fact that some countries, such as Italy, appear to have made participation in the starting phase of EMU an issue of national pride.

Tietmeyer, rejecting once again the idea that the central bank opposes EMU, said that, on the contrary, the Bundesbank's insistence on strict adherence to the Maastricht Treaty's criteria was aimed at ensuring the success of the project.
Such demands were also not simply a matter of building barriers to keep some countries out, he said.
"The argument that the call for strict meeting of the criteria should create a special 'euro-fortress' within the community is not in line with the facts," he said.
"The euro core must of course remain open for all EU countries which want and are able to participate later."
Tietmeyer rejected a French proposal for a political counterweight to the future European Central Bank, saying this was not in line with the provisions of the Maastricht Treaty on monetary union.

In a clear reference to comments from French president Jacques Chirac, Tietmeyer used the French phrases "pouvoir politique" -- political power -- and "pouvoir monetaire" monetary power, according to the text of his speech.
"Any attempts to create a 'pouvoir politique' to control or influence the 'pouvoir monetaire' would not be in line with the Treaty," Tietmeyer said.
"I hope that this will ultimately also be seen this way even in countries that do not have a similarly long tradition of an independent central bank," he added.
The Maastricht Treaty calls clearly for an independent central bank, which is entirely free from political influence and has price stability as its main priority.

Tietmeyer also warned against the precept of accepting a moderate increase in inflation if this allowed an interest rate cut which could stimulate growth, cut joblessness, help the welfare system and find answers to globalisation.
"Too low interest rates and a little more inflation are never a solution for this, neither today nor tomorrow," he said.
